title: Federal Reserve Board requests public comment on a proposal to establish a "payment account"
date_evidence: Visible dateline 'May 20, 2026' with 'For release at 4:00 p.m. EDT'; page footer 'Last Update: May 20, 2026'
key_claim: The Fed proposed a special-purpose 'payment account' that legally eligible non-bank institutions could use for the specific purpose of clearing and settling their own payments via Fedwire Funds, FedNow, the National Settlement Service and Fedwire Securities, but without intraday credit, discount-window access or interest, and without expanding legal eligibility; the comment period closes 60 days after Federal Register publication, and the Board urged Reserve Banks to pause Tier 3 master-account decisions until policy work is complete.
frame_summary: The Fed argues a limited, prefunded payment account can extend direct settlement access to non-insured institutions while keeping them in a subordinate access tier and mitigating risk to the payment system.
verbatim_quote: Payment account holders would not have access to intraday credit or the discount window, would not earn interest on balances held at a Reserve Bank, and would only have access to payment services with automated controls to prevent overdrafts.
notes: Primary anchor of the signal: the US central bank creating a new, deliberately limited tier of direct settlement access for non-banks. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Fed advances 'skinny' payment accounts for nonbanks
date_evidence: meta article:published_time: 2026-05-21T18:27:11.385; visible 'Published May 21, 2026, 2:27 p.m. EDT'
key_claim: The Board approved the payment-account proposal in a 6-to-1 vote (Governor Barr dissenting over money-laundering safeguards), raising the closing balance cap from the lesser of $500 million or 10% of total assets to a flat $1 billion; approved firms get Fedwire Funds, FedNow, the National Settlement Service and Fedwire Securities but not FedACH; the Board told Reserve Banks to pause Tier 3 master-account decisions, following the Kansas City Fed's grant of a limited-purpose account to Kraken for one year.
frame_summary: American Banker reports the skinny payment account as a concrete but deliberately restricted step toward non-bank Fed access, contested by fintechs over the ACH exclusion and by a dissenting governor over illicit-finance risk.
verbatim_quote: the Fed raised the overnight balance limit from the lesser of $500 million or 10% of total assets to a flat cap of $1 billion.
notes: Backs the numeric detail of the US account tier and the Barr dissent used in the counter-argument. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Knocking at the Fed's Door: Recent Executive Order and Regulatory Proposals Signal Broader Payment Systems Access for Fintechs and Payment Companies
date_evidence: Visible byline 'Jun 1 2026' above the article; references EO 14405 (19 May 2026) and the 20 May 2026 payment-account proposal
key_claim: Direct Fed access has long been the 'holy grail' for nonbanks; under the 2022 tiered Account Access Guidelines only one non-crypto Tier 3 institution (Numisma Bank) and one crypto firm (Kraken) have won (limited) access out of more than 8,000 active account holders; Executive Order 14405 (19 May 2026) and the payment-account proposal (20 May 2026) together open broader access, but the payment account follows current eligibility standards and is 'of little use' to firms not already eligible, excludes FedACH, and is capped at $1 billion, while courts continue to uphold Reserve Bank discretion.
frame_summary: Freshfields argues the May 2026 executive order and payment-account proposal mark a genuine opening of Fed access to nonbanks, but one still hemmed in by unchanged eligibility, the FedACH exclusion and Reserve Bank discretion upheld in court.
verbatim_quote: out of more than 8,000 active account holders
notes: Supplies the correspondent/sponsor-dependency framing and the strongest counter-argument (the tier is too restricted to change bank-dependence). Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Bank of England launches policy statement and draft rules on regulating systemic stablecoins
date_evidence: Visible 'Published on 22 June 2026' beneath the headline
key_claim: The Bank of England's systemic-stablecoin regime requires issuers to hold backing in short-term UK government debt and central bank deposits, with prompt redemption and central-bank support, and applies a temporary per-coin issuance guardrail initially set at £40 billion; the Code of Practice is to be finalised by end-2026 with regulated coins operating from 2027.
frame_summary: The BoE argues the UK's digital-money regime should be anchored in central-bank money and central-bank support, with issuance limits, keeping private stablecoins tethered to the central bank rather than free-standing.
verbatim_quote: a temporary issuance guardrail will apply to each systemic stablecoin, initially set at £40 billion.
notes: UK case: private digital money admitted only tethered to central-bank money and subject to hard quantitative limits. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Modernising money and markets - speech by Sarah Breeden
date_evidence: On-page 'Given at City Week 2026, London / Published on 19 May 2026'; the 22 June 2026 BoE press release notes list 'speech by Sarah Breeden 19 May 2026'
key_claim: The BoE has upgraded its RTGS (RT2), is building a synchronisation interface (an 18-firm Synchronisation Lab live in May 2026) and is extending settlement hours toward near-24/7 so tokenised wholesale transactions can settle in central bank money, while allowing robust privately issued money as a wholesale cash leg but keeping a low risk appetite for a significant shift away from central-bank-money settlement.
frame_summary: Breeden argues the BoE is re-engineering its own settlement infrastructure and access terms so that new forms of money settle in, or against, central bank money, keeping the central bank at the centre of the settlement layer.
verbatim_quote: enable tokenised wholesale transactions to settle in central bank money
notes: UK settlement-infrastructure evidence: access and rails are being rebuilt around central-bank-money settlement. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Eurosystem sets out comprehensive strategy for future of European payments
key_claim: The Eurosystem's payments strategy keeps central bank money at the core of retail and wholesale settlement, complemented by regulated private settlement assets such as tokenised deposits and euro stablecoins, with strategic aims of maintaining central-bank money's role, making European payments more robust and autonomous, and supporting the international role of the euro.
frame_summary: The ECB argues central bank money must remain the anchor of the euro settlement system, with private settlement assets admitted only in a complementary, regulated role.
verbatim_quote: central bank money should remain at the core, complemented by private settlement assets like tokenised deposits and stablecoins
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band). EU case: the settlement hierarchy is being codified with central-bank money at the core. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Wholesale stablecoins: fad or future?
date_evidence: meta article:published_time: 2026-05-18T13:51:11+00:00; byline 'By Philip Middleton / 18 May 2026'
key_claim: Stablecoins in issue approach just $315bn versus around $8tn in US bank deposits, and real stablecoin payment volumes are roughly $390bn (about 0.02% of global payments); the future of wholesale settlement probably belongs to tokenised deposits settled in wholesale central bank money because only central-bank settlement guarantees par and finality.
frame_summary: OMFIF argues stablecoins are marginal and structurally inferior for settlement, and that the future belongs to tokenised deposits settled in central bank money.
verbatim_quote: the value of stablecoins currently in issue approaches just $315bn compared with, for example, around $8tn held in US bank deposits alone
notes: Analytical Tier-2 voice; quantifies how small stablecoins are relative to bank and central-bank money. Quote hand-verified on the live page during sourcing (2026-07-20); sandbox egress returns 403 so the provenance audit reports UNVERIFIED, not FAIL.

title: Anchoring trust in money: innovation beyond stablecoins (Annual Economic Report 2026, Chapter III) - press release
date_evidence: meta DC.date: 2026-06-23; visible dateline 'Press release | 23 June 2026'
key_claim: The BIS argues stablecoins fall short on the 'singleness' of money and that tokenisation should be brought inside the two-tier central-bank/commercial-bank system via unified ledgers (as prototyped in Project Agora), with central-bank money as the anchor rather than routed around the system.
frame_summary: The BIS argues the next-generation monetary system should route tokenisation through central-bank money and the two-tier banking structure, not around it.
notes: Multilateral capstone: the direction of travel is to anchor new money forms in central-bank money and the two-tier system.
